en: Majjhima Nikāya 139,
Araṇavibhaṅgasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the analysis of non-conflict.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“One should not devote oneself to the pleasure of sensual desires, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial; nor should one devote oneself to self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial.

Having avoided these two extremes, monks, the Middle Way has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; it produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
One should know what is exaltation and one should know what is disparagement.”
Having understood both praise and blame, one should neither praise nor blame, but should teach only the Dhamma.
One should know the discernment of happiness;
having known the discernment of happiness, one should devote oneself to internal happiness.
One should not speak in private; one should not speak disparagingly in the presence of others.
One should speak without haste, not with haste.
One should not adhere to local dialects, nor should one override common usage. Thus it was said.
This is the summary of the analysis of non-conflict (*araṇavibhaṅga*).

“One should not devote oneself to sensual pleasure—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—nor should one devote oneself to self-mortification—which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial.
So it was said. With reference to what was this said?

Devotion to the pursuit of pleasure and joy connected with sensual desires—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state accompanied by suffering, injury, despair, and fever; it is a wrong practice.

Non-devotion to the pursuit of pleasure and joy connected with sensual desires—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state free from suffering, injury, despair, and fever; it is the right practice.
The pursuit of self-mortification is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial; this state is accompanied by suffering, harmfulness, despair, and fever, and it is a wrong practice.

The non-pursuit of the pursuit of self-mortification—which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state free from suffering, harmless, without despair, and without fever; it is the right practice.

‘One should not pursue the pleasure of sensual desires, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial; nor should one pursue self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial’—this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.

‘Not approaching either of these two extremes, the Middle Way has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; it produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna.’”
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

‘Having avoided these two extremes, the Middle Way has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; it produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna’—this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘One should know what is elevating, and one should know what is disparaging.’
"Having understood both praise and disparagement, one should neither praise nor disparage, but should teach only the Dhamma"—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?
And how, monks, does there come to be praise and disparagement, but not the teaching of the Dhamma?

‘All those who are devoted to the pursuit of the joy associated with the pleasure of sense-desires—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—are beset by suffering, injury, despair, and fever;
they have entered upon a wrong path,’—thus saying, he disparages some.

‘All those who are not devoted to the pursuit of the joy associated with the pleasure of sense-desires—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—are free from suffering, injury, despair, and fever; they have entered upon the right path.’—Thus he disparages some.
Saying this, some praise them.
Saying, "All those who are devoted to the pursuit of self-mortification—which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—are all subject to suffering, injury, despair, and fever;
they have entered upon a wrong path," saying this, some disparage them.

‘All those who do not devote themselves to the pursuit of self-mortification— which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial— are free from suffering, free from affliction, free from despair, free from fever,
and have entered upon the right path’— thus saying, he encourages some.
‘All those by whom the fetter of existence has not been abandoned are possessed of suffering, possessed of affliction, possessed of despair, possessed of fever, and have entered upon the wrong path.’
Saying this, some disparage others. Saying,
"Whosoever have abandoned the fetter of existence, they are all free from suffering, free from affliction, free from despair, free from fever, and are practicing rightly"—
saying this, some exalt others.
In this way, monks, there is both praise and disparagement, but not the teaching of the Dhamma.
And how, monks, is there neither praise nor disparagement, but the teaching of the Dhamma?

“Those who are devoted to the pursuit of pleasure connected with sensual desires—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—all of them are subject to suffering, injury, despair, and fever; they have entered upon the wrong path. This, monks, is neither praise nor disparagement, but the teaching of the Dhamma.
He does not say:
"This practice is indeed painful, harmful, distressing, and feverish;
it is a wrong course of conduct."
Speaking thus, he teaches only the Dhamma:

“Those who do not devote themselves to the pursuit of happiness connected with sensual pleasures— which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial— but are all free from suffering, free from affliction, free from despair, free from fever, and are practicing rightly”— he does not speak in this way.
‘Non-attachment, moreover, is this state that is without suffering, without affliction, without despair, and without fever;
it is the right practice’— speaking thus, he teaches only the Dhamma.

‘All those who are devoted to the pursuit of self-mortification—which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—are themselves accompanied by suffering, injury, despair, and fever, and have entered upon a wrong path’—he does not say this.
Rather, he says:
‘This practice is indeed a state accompanied by suffering, injury, despair, and fever.’
‘Wrong practice’— saying this, he teaches only the Dhamma.

‘Those who do not devote themselves to the pursuit of self-mortification— which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial— all of them are practicing rightly, being free from suffering, free from affliction, free from despair, and free from fever.’
He does not say:
"Non-inquiry is this state that is without suffering, without affliction, without despair, without fever;
it is the right practice."
Speaking thus, he teaches only the Dhamma.
He does not say: "Whosoever have not abandoned the fetter of existence, they are all beset by suffering, affliction, despair, and fever, and have entered upon the wrong path."
‘When the fetter of existence has not been abandoned, existence itself has not been abandoned’— speaking thus, he teaches only the Dhamma.
‘Whoever has abandoned the fetter of existence, all of them are free from suffering, free from affliction, free from despair, free from fever, and have entered upon the right path.’
He does not say this:
"When the fetter of existence is abandoned, existence itself is also abandoned.
Speaking thus, he teaches only the Dhamma.
“Thus, monks, there is neither exalting nor disparaging, but only the teaching of the Dhamma.
‘One should know what exalting is and one should know what disparaging is;
having known exalting and having known disparaging, one should neither exalt nor disparage, but should teach only the Dhamma.’”
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this:
“One should know the determination of pleasure;
having known the determination of pleasure, one should devote oneself to internal happiness.”
Thus indeed it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure.
What five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … [and so forth].
Tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure,
and provocative of lust— these, monks, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
“Monks, whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent upon these five cords of sensual pleasure, this is called sensual pleasure, a filthy pleasure, a vulgar pleasure, an ignoble pleasure.
‘It is not to be cultivated, it is not to be developed, it is not to be practiced frequently; one should fear this pleasure,’ I say.

Here, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a monk enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.”
With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought,

and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration. And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous … [as above] … he enters and dwells in the third jhāna … [as above] … he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This is called the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, and the happiness of enlightenment.
"It should be cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently; one should not fear this happiness," I say.
"One should know the discernment of happiness."
‘Having understood the determination of pleasure, one should devote oneself to internal happiness’—
this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘One should not speak in private, nor should one say what is disparaging in the presence [of others]’—
Thus indeed it was said.
With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, monks, if one should know that a private conversation is untrue, incorrect, and not conducive to the goal, one should not speak that private conversation even with permission.
If one should know that a private reproach is true, factual, and unbeneficial, one should train oneself not to speak it.
But if one should know that a private reproach is true, factual, and beneficial, one should be discerning of the proper time to speak that private reproach.
In this regard, monks, if one should know that a face-to-face reproach is untrue, unfactual, and unbeneficial, one should not, even with courtesy, utter that face-to-face reproach.
One should train not to speak even that private criticism which one knows to be true, factual, and unbeneficial.
However, regarding that private criticism which one knows to be true, factual, and beneficial, one should know the proper time to speak it in the person's presence. Thus:
"One should not speak in secret, nor should one utter what is not private criticism in the presence of others."
Thus, that which was said—"one should speak unhurriedly, not hurriedly"—was said with reference to this. And as for what was said:
"Why was this said? It was said with reference to this.

In this regard, monks, when one speaks in haste, the body becomes weary, the mind is disturbed, the voice is strained, and the throat is afflicted; furthermore, what is spoken in haste is indistinct and unintelligible.

In this regard, monks, when one speaks without haste, the body does not become weary, the mind is not disturbed, the voice is not strained, and the throat is not afflicted; furthermore, what is spoken without haste is distinct and intelligible.
"One should speak without haste, not in haste"—this is how it should be.
Thus, that which was said— "One should not adhere to local dialects, nor should one override common usage"— this was said with reference to this.
And as for what was said, with reference to what was it said?
And how, monks, is there adherence to local dialects and overstepping conventional terminology? Here, monks, regarding the very same thing,
people in some regions perceive it as ‘a bowl’ (*pāti*), they perceive it as ‘a vessel’ (*patta*), they perceive it as ‘a cup’ (*vitta*),
they perceive it as ‘a saucer’ (*sarāva*), they perceive it as ‘a dish’ (*dhāropa*), or they perceive it as ‘a platter’ (*poṇa*).
They perceive it; they perceive it as ‘Pisīlavat.
Thus, in whatever way they perceive it in those various regions, in that very way they adhere to it with persistence and grasping, and they declare:
“This alone is the truth, all else is false.”
"Thus, monks, there is adherence to local dialects and overstepping conventional terminology.
And how, monks, is there non-adherence to local dialects and no overstepping of conventional terminology?
Here, monks, regarding the very same thing, people in some districts perceive it as 'a bowl' (*pātī*), while in others they perceive it as 'a vessel' (*patta*)."
They perceive it as ‘wealth,’ they perceive it as ‘a bowl,’ they perceive it as ‘a lid,’ they perceive it as ‘a base,’ they perceive it as ‘a stand.
Thus, in whatever way people in various regions perceive it, thinking, “It is surely with reference to this that these venerable ones speak,” he speaks accordingly without misapprehending it.
"Thus, monks, there is non-adherence to local dialects and no overstepping of common usage.
'One should not adhere to local dialects; one should not override common usage'—this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this."

In this regard, monks, that pursuit of the enjoyment of pleasure connected with sensual desires—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state accompanied by suffering, accompanied by harm, accompanied by despair, and accompanied by fever;
it is a wrong practice.
Therefore, this state is fraught with peril.

In this regard, monks, that non-devotion to the pursuit of joy connected with sensual pleasures—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state free from suffering, free from affliction, free from despair, and free from fever;
it is the right practice.
Therefore, this state is without conflict.

In this regard, monks, that devotion to self-mortification which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial is a state accompanied by suffering, accompanied by harm, accompanied by despair, and accompanied by fever;
it is a wrong practice.
Therefore, this state is with conflict.

In this regard, monks, that which is non-devotion to the pursuit of self-mortification—which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state that is without suffering, without affliction, without despair, and without fever;
it is the right practice.
Therefore, this state is free from conflict.
In this regard, monks, that middle way realized by the Tathāgata— which produces vision, produces knowledge,
and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna— is a Dhamma that is without suffering,
without affliction, without despair, and without fever.
It is the right way of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is free from conflict.

In this regard, monks, that which consists of praising and disparaging, rather than teaching the Dhamma, is a Dhamma accompanied by suffering, accompanied by injury, accompanied by vexation, and accompanied by fever.
It is a wrong course of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is a refuge.
In that regard, monks, that teaching of the Dhamma which involves neither exalting nor disparaging—this Dhamma is without suffering, without affliction, without despair, and without fever.
It is the right way of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is without conflict.

In this regard, monks, that which is sensual pleasure, filthy pleasure, the pleasure of the vulgar, the ignoble pleasure—this Dhamma is accompanied by suffering, accompanied by harm, accompanied by despair, and accompanied by fever.
It is a wrong course of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is a refuge.

In that regard, monks, whatever is the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, and the happiness of enlightenment—this Dhamma is without suffering, without affliction, without despair, and without fever.
It is the right way of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is free from conflict.

In that regard, monks, whatever secret talk there may be that is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial—that Dhamma is accompanied by suffering, accompanied by harm, accompanied by distress, and accompanied by fever.
It is a wrong course of practice.
Therefore, this phenomenon is accompanied by peril.

In that regard, monks, whatever private reproach there is that is true, factual, and unbeneficial—that phenomenon is accompanied by suffering, accompanied by harm, accompanied by despair, and accompanied by fever.
It is a wrong course of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is a source of refuge.
In that regard, monks, whatever private speech there may be that is factual, true, and beneficial—that Dhamma is free from suffering, non-injurious, non-afflictive, and non-feverish.
It is the right way of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is free from conflict.

In that regard, monks, whatever face-to-face accusation is untrue, incorrect, and not conducive to welfare—this Dhamma is accompanied by suffering, accompanied by harm, accompanied by distress, and accompanied by fever.
It is a wrong course of practice.
Therefore, this dhamma is with conflict.

In that regard, monks, whatever face-to-face criticism there is that is factual, truthful, and unbeneficial—this dhamma is accompanied by suffering, accompanied by harm, accompanied by distress, and accompanied by fever.
It is a wrong course of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is a refuge.
In that regard, monks, that which is spoken in one's presence—being true, factual, and beneficial—is a Dhamma that is without suffering, without injury, without despair, and without fever.
It is the right way of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is free from conflict.
In that regard, monks, as for this speech of one who is hurrying: this Dhamma is accompanied by suffering, accompanied by injury, accompanied by despair, and accompanied by fever.
It is a wrong course of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is a refuge.
In that regard, monks, as for this speech of one who is not hasty: this Dhamma is without suffering, without affliction, without despair, and without fever.
It is the right way of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is free from conflict.

In this regard, monks, whatever adherence to local dialects and insistence on common parlance, that Dhamma is accompanied by suffering, accompanied by harm, accompanied by despair, and accompanied by fever.
It is a wrong course of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is a refuge.

In that regard, monks, that which is non-adherence to local dialects and non-transgression regarding conventional designations—this Dhamma is without suffering, without affliction, without despair, and without fever.
It is the right way of practice.
Therefore, this Dhamma is free from conflict.
Therefore, monks, [you should train yourselves thus]: ‘We shall know the Dhamma that leads to conflict, and we shall know the Dhamma that is free from conflict.’”
“‘Having understood the state with conflict and having understood the state without conflict, we shall practice the way that is without conflict’—thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
And the clansman Subhūti, monks, has practiced the way that is without conflict.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The bhikkhus were uplifted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The ninth discourse, the *Araṇavibhaṅgasutta*, is concluded.
